name: Clustering Papers by Meaning
title: Clustering Papers by Meaning
answer: Clustering papers by meaning groups research papers according to what they actually argue, find, or assume, rather than by shared keywords, authors, or citation counts. In citation mapping and discovery, this turns a flat list of references into a map of related ideas. The scope includes identifying emerging themes, separating near-duplicate work, and showing how a field's questions connect. On this site, the practice applies to a curated library of 135 research papers, where each paper can belong to more than one meaning-based cluster.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Clustering papers by meaning groups research papers according to what they actually argue, find, or assume, rather than by shared keywords, authors, or citation counts. In citation mapping and discovery, this turns a flat list of references into a map of related ideas. The scope includes identifying emerging themes, separating near-duplicate work, and showing how a field's questions connect. On this site, the practice applies to a curated library of 135 research papers, where each paper can belong to more than one meaning-based cluster.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on standard text embedding models that convert paper titles, abstracts, and extracted claims into dense vectors. These vectors are stored in a vector index that supports fast nearest neighbor search, which is the core operation for clustering. For a corpus of this size, a single modern CPU or a small GPU is sufficient, and no specialized hardware is required. The index can be rebuilt when new papers are added, and the embeddings can be cached so that repeated clustering runs do not recompute them from scratch.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: First, the text of each paper is cleaned and split into meaningful units, often the abstract or the individual claims extracted from the work. Each unit is passed through an embedding model to produce a vector that captures its meaning. A clustering algorithm such as HDBSCAN or k-means then groups nearby vectors, with the number of clusters either set by the user or discovered from the data. After clustering, each group is labeled by its most central terms, its most representative paper, or a short phrase generated from the cluster's contents. The result is a set of meaning-based groups that can be reviewed against the original papers.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Provenance is the main governance concern: a cluster is only useful if every paper in it can be traced back to its original source. This site links each clustered item to the original paper, never to a third-party search tool. Rights and risk also include the possibility that an embedding model carries bias from its training data, which can place papers in misleading groups. Reviewers should treat clusters as suggestions to verify, not as final classifications. No cluster label or grouping should be presented as a substitute for reading the underlying work.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The practice is moving toward claim-level clustering, where individual findings rather than whole papers are grouped, because a single paper often makes several distinct arguments. Hybrid methods that combine semantic similarity with citation structure are also likely, since citations capture influence that meaning alone can miss. As the library grows beyond its current 135 papers, the main challenge will be keeping clusters interpretable at scale. Interactive maps that let a researcher zoom from a broad theme to a single claim are a natural next step.
